questions.explanation: St Patrick (Ireland) is a diagonal red cross on a white ground. St George (England) is an upright red cross on a white ground. St Andrew (Scotland) is a diagonal white cross on a blue ground. The red dragon is the Welsh flag.

questions.question: Roughly how many people lived in the British Empire at its height in the Victorian period?
questions.explanation: The Empire had an estimated population of more than 400 million. 'About 13 million' relates to the number of British citizens who emigrated between 1853 and 1913 — relevant to emigration, not the Empire's population.

questions.question: The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 promoted which policy?
questions.explanation: Repealing the Corn Laws in 1846 promoted free trade by allowing cheaper grain imports. Protectionism is the opposite. Nationalisation relates to the post-1945 government, and devolution to powers for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

questions.question: The Crimean War (1853–56) was fought against which country?
questions.explanation: Britain, with Turkey and France, fought against Russia in the Crimean War. France was an ally in this war, not the enemy. Germany and Spain were not involved.

questions.question: Queen Victoria introduced which medal during the Crimean War?
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria introduced the Victoria Cross to honour acts of valour. The other awards are real honours but not the one she introduced during the Crimean War.

questions.question: In the 19th century, a famine in Ireland was caused by the failure of which crop?
questions.explanation: The Irish famine was caused by the failure of the potato crop, on which many people depended; a million died and a million and a half emigrated. The other crops were not the cause of the famine.

questions.question: Which author, born in India, wrote The Jungle Book and the poem 'If'?
questions.explanation: Rudyard Kipling, born in India, wrote The Jungle Book and 'If', and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907. Dickens, Stevenson and Hardy were other notable authors but not the writer of these works.

questions.question: Whose assassination in 1914 helped trigger the First World War?
questions.explanation: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria on 28 June 1914 triggered the chain of events leading to WWI. The other figures were involved in 20th-century history but were not the assassinated trigger.

questions.question: In the First World War, Britain fought as part of which side?
questions.explanation: Britain was part of the Allied Powers (with France, Russia and others). The Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman Empire) were the enemy in WWI. The Axis relates to WWII, and the Warsaw Pact to the Cold War.

questions.question: The 1916 uprising against British rule in Dublin was known as what?
questions.explanation: The Easter Rising of 1916 was an uprising against the British in Dublin. The Glorious Revolution (1688) brought William of Orange to the throne. The Jacobite Rising supported the exiled Stuarts. The Peasants' Revolt was a medieval event.

questions.question: In which year did the world enter the 'Great Depression'?
questions.explanation: The Great Depression began in 1929, causing mass unemployment in parts of the UK. 1918 is the end of WWI, 1939 the start of WWII, and 1945 the end of WWII.

questions.question: When did the BBC begin the world's first regular television service?
questions.explanation: The BBC began the world's first regular television service in 1936. It started radio broadcasts in 1922 — so 1922 is relevant to radio. 1969 and 1990 relate to other events (voting age; the first web transfer).

questions.question: In WWII, the Axis powers were Germany, Italy and which other country?
questions.explanation: The Axis powers were Germany, Italy and Japan. Russia (the Soviet Union) was invaded by Germany and joined the Allies. France and Poland were on the Allied side.

questions.question: The D-Day landings of 6 June 1944 took place where?
questions.explanation: Allied forces landed in Normandy on D-Day (6 June 1944). Dunkirk relates to the 1940 evacuation. Berlin was the German capital, reached later. Sicily saw earlier Allied action in Italy but was not the D-Day location.

questions.question: Which British scientist developed radar?
questions.explanation: Sir Robert Watson-Watt, a Scotsman, developed radar. John Logie Baird developed television. Sir Frank Whittle developed the jet engine. Sir Bernard Lovell built the Jodrell Bank radio telescope.

questions.question: Who developed the jet engine in Britain in the 1930s?
questions.explanation: Sir Frank Whittle, an RAF engineer officer, developed the jet engine. Sir Christopher Cockerell invented the hovercraft. James Goodfellow invented the cash-dispensing ATM. Sir Peter Mansfield co-invented the MRI scanner.

questions.question: Who invented the hovercraft in the 1950s?
questions.explanation: Sir Christopher Cockerell invented the hovercraft. Sir Frank Whittle developed the jet engine. Alan Turing devised the Turing machine. John MacLeod co-discovered insulin.

questions.question: The first cash-dispensing ATM was put into use by Barclays Bank in 1967 in which London area?
questions.explanation: The first ATM, invented by James Goodfellow, was installed by Barclays in Enfield, north London, in 1967. Greenwich, Canterbury and Stratford are associated with other landmarks and events.

questions.question: The world's first 'test-tube baby' (from IVF) was born in 1978 in which town?
questions.explanation: IVF was pioneered by Sir Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe, and the first test-tube baby was born in Oldham, Lancashire, in 1978. The other places are associated with other scientific work.

questions.question: Dolly the sheep, the first cloned mammal, was created in which year?
questions.explanation: Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996 by a team led by Sir Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell. 1953 relates to the discovery of DNA's structure, 1978 to the first IVF baby, and 1990 to the first web transfer.

questions.question: In 1947, independence was granted to nine countries, including which of these?
questions.explanation: In 1947, independence was granted to nine countries, including India, Pakistan and Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). Other African and Caribbean colonies gained independence over the following 20 years, so Kenya and Nigeria came later.

questions.question: Which Prime Minister gave the famous 'wind of change' speech about decolonisation?
questions.explanation: Harold Macmillan, PM in the late 1950s, gave the 'wind of change' speech. Clement Attlee led the 1945 government, Churchill led Britain in WWII, and Thatcher became PM in 1979.

questions.question: The Education Act 1944 ('the Butler Act') introduced what in England and Wales?
questions.explanation: The Butler Act (1944) introduced free secondary education and the primary/secondary division. The NHS was created in 1948 under a different reform. The other options are not what the Act introduced.

questions.question: In 1948, people from where were invited to come and work in Britain?
questions.explanation: In 1948, people from the West Indies were invited to come and help rebuild Britain. Later, workers were also recruited from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. The other regions were not part of this post-war recruitment.

questions.question: Which two famous pop groups were prominent in the 'Swinging Sixties'?
options: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones
questions.answer: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones
questions.explanation: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones were prominent in the 1960s and continue to influence music. The other bands are real British acts but are not the two named in the handbook for the 'Swinging Sixties'.

questions.question: In which year did the UK join the European Economic Community (EEC)?
questions.explanation: The UK joined the EEC in 1973. 1957 is when the EEC was founded by the Treaty of Rome. 2020 is when the UK left the EU (Brexit). 1999 relates to devolution.

questions.question: Margaret Thatcher trained in which two professions before entering politics?
questions.explanation: Margaret Thatcher, the grocer's daughter from Grantham, trained as a chemist and a lawyer. The other professions are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: The Conservative government from 2015 to 2024 included several Prime Ministers. Which of these was one of them?
questions.explanation: Conservative PMs in that period included David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak. Tony Blair and Gordon Brown were earlier Labour PMs, and Keir Starmer became Labour PM in 2024.

questions.question: Who was the organist at Westminster Abbey and developed a distinctly British musical style?
questions.explanation: Henry Purcell was the organist at Westminster Abbey and developed a distinct British style. Handel was German-born and wrote Messiah. Holst wrote The Planets, and Elgar the Pomp and Circumstance Marches.

questions.question: Gilbert and Sullivan are famous for writing which kind of work?
questions.explanation: Gilbert and Sullivan wrote comic operas such as HMS Pinafore, The Pirates of Penzance and The Mikado. Detective novels relate to Agatha Christie and Conan Doyle. War poetry relates to Wilfred Owen and Siegfried Sassoon.

questions.question: Which composer's works include Peter Grimes and Billy Budd, and who founded the Aldeburgh festival?
questions.explanation: Benjamin Britten wrote Peter Grimes and Billy Budd and founded the Aldeburgh festival. Walton wrote Façade; Vaughan Williams was influenced by folk music; Purcell was a much earlier composer.

questions.question: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is best known for showcasing what?
questions.explanation: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe showcases mainly theatre and comedy, often experimental. Classical painting relates to galleries and the Turner Prize. Motor racing and horse racing are sports, not the Fringe.

questions.question: Which landscape painter is most famous for works of Dedham Vale?
questions.explanation: John Constable is famous for painting Dedham Vale on the Suffolk–Essex border. Thomas Gainsborough painted portraits in country settings. Henry Moore was a sculptor. David Hockney is associated with pop art.

questions.question: Which architect designed the Queen's House at Greenwich and the Banqueting House in Whitehall?
questions.explanation: Inigo Jones designed the Queen's House at Greenwich and the Banqueting House. Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral. Robert Adam is relevant to the Royal Crescent in Bath. Sir Edwin Lutyens designed the Cenotaph.

questions.question: Which 18th-century figure designed landscapes so they appeared natural, and often said a place had 'capabilities'?
questions.explanation: Lancelot 'Capability' Brown designed natural-looking landscapes around country houses. Gertrude Jekyll designed colourful gardens, often with Lutyens. Robert Adam was an architect, and Sir Norman Foster is a modern architect.

questions.question: Which British author wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations?
questions.explanation: Charles Dickens wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, and created characters such as Scrooge and Mr Micawber. Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice. Thomas Hardy wrote Far from the Madding Crowd. Graham Greene wrote Brighton Rock.

questions.question: Which poet wrote Paradise Lost?
questions.explanation: John Milton wrote Paradise Lost. William Wordsworth wrote 'The Daffodils'. William Blake wrote 'The Tyger'. Lord Byron wrote 'She Walks in Beauty'.

questions.question: What is the day after Christmas Day called?
questions.explanation: Boxing Day (26 December) is the day after Christmas and a public holiday. New Year's Day is 1 January. Shrove Tuesday is the day before Lent. The other option is a distractor.

questions.question: The Jewish festival remembered by lighting candles on a menorah over eight days is called what?
questions.explanation: Hanukkah is a Jewish festival lasting eight days, marked by lighting a menorah. Diwali is a Hindu and Sikh festival. Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival. Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan for Muslims.

questions.question: Vaisakhi, celebrated on 14 April, is a festival for which faith?
questions.explanation: Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival celebrating the founding of the Khalsa, on 14 April. Diwali is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs. Eid festivals are Muslim, and Hanukkah is Jewish.

questions.question: Mothering Sunday falls when?
options: On the third Sunday in June
questions.explanation: Mothering Sunday (Mother's Day) is the Sunday three weeks before Easter. The third Sunday in June is Father's Day. 14 February is Valentine's Day, and 1 April is April Fool's Day.

questions.question: Rented land where people grow fruit and vegetables is called what?
questions.explanation: An allotment is rented land for growing fruit and vegetables. A croft was a small Scottish farm, relevant to the Highland Clearances. A plantation relates to settlement in Ulster. A 'common' is a different kind of shared land.

questions.question: The satirical magazine first published in the 1840s was called what?
questions.explanation: Punch was first published in the 1840s and was the most famous satirical magazine. Private Eye continues the tradition of satire today. Hansard is the official record of parliamentary proceedings, not a satirical magazine.

questions.question: In which year was the National Trust founded?
questions.explanation: The National Trust was founded in 1895 by three volunteers. 1984 relates to the establishment of the Turner Prize. 1945 and 1707 relate to other events (post-war government; Act of Union).

questions.question: The clock tower housing Big Ben was renamed in 2012 in honour of the Queen. What is it now called?
questions.explanation: The tower was named Elizabeth Tower in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee in 2012. Big Ben is actually the nickname of the great bell. The Shard is a separate modern skyscraper.

questions.question: The spiritual leader of the Church of England is who?
questions.explanation: The Archbishop of Canterbury is the spiritual leader of the Church of England. The monarch is its head. The Moderator chairs the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland. The Pope leads the Roman Catholic Church.

questions.question: Which flower is associated with Northern Ireland?
questions.explanation: The shamrock is associated with Northern Ireland. The daffodil is associated with Wales, the rose with England, and the thistle with Scotland.

questions.question: The Paralympic Games have their origins in the work of Dr Ludwig Guttman at which hospital?
questions.explanation: Dr Ludwig Guttman's work at Stoke Mandeville hospital in Buckinghamshire led to the Paralympics. St Thomas' is relevant to Florence Nightingale's nursing school. The other hospitals are distractors here.

questions.question: Sir Steve Redgrave won gold medals in which sport across five consecutive Olympic Games?
questions.explanation: Sir Steve Redgrave won rowing golds in five consecutive Olympics. Cycling relates to Sir Chris Hoy and Sir Bradley Wiggins. Athletics relates to figures like Mo Farah, and sailing to Dame Ellen MacArthur.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
questions.explanation: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland. Cardiff is the capital of Wales, Edinburgh of Scotland. Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland, which is a separate country and not part of the UK.

questions.question: What is the National Anthem of the UK?
questions.explanation: The National Anthem is 'God Save the King (or Queen)'. 'Land of Hope and Glory' is played at the Last Night of the Proms. 'Rule Britannia' and 'Jerusalem' are patriotic songs but not the national anthem.

questions.question: Which court in Scotland hears the most serious cases, such as murder?
questions.explanation: In Scotland the most serious cases, such as murder, are heard at the High Court with a judge and jury. The Sheriff Court hears less serious cases. Magistrates' Courts and County Courts operate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, not Scotland.
